lesson.title: Regular and Irregular Polygons

steps.say: Hi friend! It's Ms. Yuanyuan. Yesterday I was walking past a park in Burnaby and I saw two signs. One was a stop sign — eight sides, and every single side looked exactly the same length. The other was a big arrow sign pointing to the playground — also a closed shape with straight sides, but its sides were all different lengths. Both are polygons! Today we'll learn how to tell these two families apart.

visual.caption: Two signs, two kinds of polygons

steps.say: First, what makes a shape a polygon at all? A polygon needs three things: it is closed, so you can trace all the way around and come back to where you started with no gaps. It is made only of straight sides. And the sides don't cross each other. So a triangle is a polygon, a square is a polygon, but a circle is not, because it has no straight sides.

visual.caption: A triangle: closed, straight sides — a polygon!

steps.say: Now here is the big idea. A regular polygon has two things true at once: all its sides are the same length, AND all its corners, called angles, are the same size. If even one of those is not true, we call it irregular. Both words are fine — irregular does not mean broken, it just means the sides or corners are not all twins.

visual.caption: A square: 4 equal sides, 4 equal corners — regular

steps.say: Let's do our first example together. This rectangle is five centimetres long and two centimetres wide. Are all four sides equal? No — two sides are five centimetres and two sides are two centimetres. So even though all four corners are perfect right angles, the sides are not all the same. This rectangle is an irregular polygon.

visual.caption: Sides 5, 2, 5, 2 — not all equal, so irregular

steps.say: Careful, here's a tricky one! This triangle has a base of six centimetres and a height of four centimetres, and its three sides measure six, five, and five centimetres. Two sides match, but one doesn't. Remember our rule — all sides must be equal. Six is not five, so this triangle is irregular. Only a triangle with all three sides equal, like six, six, and six, would be regular.

visual.caption: Sides 6, 5, 5 — one side is different, so irregular

steps.say: Now let's sort some shapes by counting sides too, because that's the other attribute we use. Here's a little table of four shapes from my classroom. Look how we can sort them two ways at once: by how many sides, and by regular or irregular. A stop sign has eight equal sides, so it's a regular octagon. A hockey rink outline is a shape with unequal sides, so it's irregular.

visual.caption: Count the sides first, then check if they're all equal

steps.say: Here's something beautiful from right here in Canada. Yup'ik artists create border patterns along the edges of clothing and baskets, repeating polygon shapes over and over. Imagine a border strip that repeats a pattern of one regular square, then two irregular triangles, again and again. If that pattern repeats four times, how many shapes in total? Each repeat has one plus two, which is three shapes. Four repeats times three shapes equals twelve shapes on the border.

visual.caption: 4 repeats of 3 shapes = 12 polygons in the border

steps.say: So here's our whole lesson in one breath. Every polygon is closed with straight sides. Then ask yourself two questions: are all the sides equal, and are all the corners equal? If both answers are yes, it's regular. If either answer is no, it's irregular. That's it — you've got it!

visual.caption: All sides 4 cm, all corners equal — regular!

lesson.answer: A polygon is regular only when ALL its sides are equal AND all its corners are equal — otherwise it's irregular.

practice.question: Mia is making a garden border in her Kelowna backyard with a shape that has 6 straight sides. She measures them: 3 m, 3 m, 3 m, 3 m, 3 m, and 3 m, and all six corners are the same size. Is her hexagon regular or irregular? Then, what is the total length of her border?
practice.answer: It is a REGULAR hexagon, because all 6 sides are equal (3 m each) and all 6 corners are equal. The border is 6 × 3 = 18 metres long.
